elements.name: Standing stone
elements.definition: A large stone set upright, singly or as one part of a larger monument.
elements.loadPath: Its weight passes to the buried or supported base; stability also depends on embedment and the ground.
limitations: Function and meaning require site-specific archaeological evidence.

elements.name: Post and lintel
elements.definition: Vertical supports carry a horizontal spanning member.
elements.loadPath: The lintel bends between supports; reactions pass through the posts to the ground.
limitations: A visual span does not establish material strength or joint stability.

elements.name: Stepped pyramid
elements.definition: A pyramid-like mass formed by successively smaller raised stages.
elements.loadPath: In a solid massing idealization, upper stages bear on lower stages and the foundation.
limitations: Egyptian chronology and function must not be transferred to superficially similar monuments elsewhere.

elements.name: Smooth-sided pyramid
elements.definition: A pyramidal exterior whose faces form continuous inclined planes.
elements.loadPath: The mass bears downward through its internal construction; visible faces alone do not reveal that construction.
limitations: Internal chambers and masonry arrangement require separate archaeological evidence.

elements.name: Terraced platform
elements.definition: Raised stages create successive horizontal surfaces and setbacks.
elements.loadPath: Upper masses bear through supporting construction; retained fills and edge walls introduce separate stability questions.
limitations: Material composition and construction sequence vary by site.

elements.name: Monumental stair
elements.definition: A conspicuous sequence of treads and risers organizes ascent through a monumental setting.
elements.loadPath: Each step transfers use and self-weight to its support or underlying mass.
limitations: Historic ceremonial dimensions do not imply safe modern public access.

elements.name: Column
elements.definition: A relatively slender upright member, often articulated as base, shaft and capital.
elements.loadPath: Compression and possible bending pass through the shaft to its base.
limitations: Slenderness, eccentricity and joints influence stability.

elements.name: Capital
elements.definition: The shaped head of a column mediates between its shaft and supported construction.
elements.loadPath: Bearing spreads or redirects through the capital into the column below.
limitations: The three Greek orders have distinct histories and details; one generic capital cannot represent all of them.

elements.name: Entablature
elements.definition: The horizontal assembly above classical columns, commonly organized into architrave, frieze and cornice.
elements.loadPath: Spanning and supported parts transfer their loads to the columns; ornament need not perform the same structural role.
limitations: Its composition and proportions vary across periods and orders.

elements.name: True arch
elements.definition: A curved span whose pieces work together through compression rather than successive horizontal overhangs.
elements.loadPath: Compression follows the arch toward its supports, producing vertical reactions and outward thrust.
limitations: Support restraint, contact and geometry must be analysed; an arch outline is not proof of stability.

elements.name: Voussoir
elements.definition: A wedge-shaped unit in an arch, vault or dome.
elements.loadPath: Contact forces transfer between adjacent units and toward the supports.
limitations: A modelled wedge does not specify mortar, joint friction or fabrication tolerances.

elements.name: Barrel vault
elements.definition: An arch-like cross-section extended along a direction to cover a longitudinal space.
elements.loadPath: Compression carries roof loading to the side supports, which must also resist lateral thrust.
limitations: Openings and changes of section alter the load path.

elements.name: Dome
elements.definition: A curved covering over a plan, often represented schematically by part of a sphere.
elements.loadPath: Forces travel through the curved surface to its supporting ring, walls or piers; the pattern depends on shape and loading.
limitations: A hemispherical diagram does not describe every dome or establish membrane-only behaviour.

elements.name: Oculus
elements.definition: A circular opening; in dome studies, the opening at or near the crown.
elements.loadPath: An opening interrupts the surface, so forces must pass around its boundary.
limitations: Daylight, weather, drainage and ring behaviour require their own design.

elements.name: Pier
elements.definition: A substantial upright support receiving an arch, vault, beam or other supported construction.
elements.loadPath: Vertical force and any thrust or bending continue to the foundation through the pier.
limitations: A pier is not automatically adequate against lateral thrust or settlement.

elements.name: Pointed arch
elements.definition: An arch profile whose two sides meet at an apex rather than a continuously rounded crown.
elements.loadPath: Compression still requires suitable supports; the thrust depends on rise, span, thickness and load.
limitations: Pointed shape alone does not guarantee higher capacity or lower thrust.

elements.name: Rib vault
elements.definition: A vaulted covering organized by projecting ribs with web surfaces between them.
elements.loadPath: Ribs, webs and adjoining fabric interact to transfer forces toward springing supports.
limitations: A rib-only diagram omits web action and is not a complete structural model.

elements.name: Flying buttress
elements.definition: An external arched support bridges from upper building fabric toward a detached or outer buttress.
elements.loadPath: It conveys lateral thrust toward a resisting outer mass and its foundation.
limitations: Its working geometry depends on the building, construction phases and continuing movement.

elements.name: Vimana in the Chola context
elements.definition: The sanctum tower of the southern Indian temple examples described here, often articulated in diminishing tiers.
elements.loadPath: The masonry mass transfers weight through its underlying shrine construction and supports.
limitations: Terminology has broader textual uses; this entry is scoped to UNESCO's Tamil Chola examples, not gopuram gateways or all Indian temples.

elements.name: Corbel
elements.definition: A projecting masonry block supports a feature or participates in successive projecting courses.
elements.loadPath: The projection transfers bearing and bending effects into the supported wall or backing.
limitations: A corbelled opening has a different construction principle from a voussoir arch.

elements.name: Timber post-and-beam frame
elements.definition: Timber uprights and horizontal members form the main supporting framework.
elements.loadPath: Roof loads pass through beams and connections into posts; lateral resistance depends on the complete assembly.
limitations: Joinery, member grading and regional practice must be established separately.

elements.name: Dougong bracket set
elements.definition: An assembly of bearing blocks and arms mediates between roof construction and supports in Chinese timber architecture.
elements.loadPath: Its pieces transmit roof forces toward columns or walls through their contacts and connections.
limitations: Historical bracket types, proportions and mechanical behaviour vary; decorative imitation is not equivalent to a working assembly.

elements.name: Purlin
elements.definition: A longitudinal roof member supports roof decking or intermediate roofing elements.
elements.loadPath: It spans between roof supports and transfers their distributed loading into the main frame.
limitations: Its position and supported elements depend on the roof system.

elements.name: Courtyard
elements.definition: An open space enclosed or framed by surrounding building parts.
elements.loadPath: A courtyard is a spatial arrangement, not itself a structural member; adjacent fabric has separate load paths.
limitations: Climate performance and social meaning are context-specific.

elements.name: Arcade
elements.definition: A sequence of arches carried by columns or piers, often forming an edge or passage.
elements.loadPath: Each arch transfers forces to its supports; adjacent bays may share supports and thrust.
limitations: Changing or removing a bay can change the behaviour of neighbouring supports.

elements.name: Diagrid
elements.definition: A structural network of diagonal members forms a triangulated building frame or envelope.
elements.loadPath: Diagonal members and ties work with the rest of the building to carry gravity and lateral effects.
limitations: Connections, core interaction, fire protection and drift cannot be inferred from a facade pattern.

elements.name: Gridshell
elements.definition: A curved grid of slender members acts collectively as a shell-like roof structure when adequately stabilized.
elements.loadPath: The interconnected grid and boundary system distribute forces toward supports; bending and bracing remain relevant.
limitations: A curved quadrilateral lattice without a resolved bracing and connection design is only geometry.

elements.name: Space frame
elements.definition: Members and nodes form a three-dimensional structural network, often with more than one chord layer.
elements.loadPath: Forces pass through the connected members and nodes toward supports in several directions.
limitations: Member ends, node eccentricity, buckling and support conditions require engineered details.

elements.name: Truss
elements.definition: A framework arranged to carry loading through connected chords and web members, commonly using triangles.
elements.loadPath: An ideal pin-jointed model carries axial member forces; real joints can introduce bending and eccentricity.
limitations: The axial-force idealization requires appropriate joints, load positions and stability assumptions.

elements.name: Shell
elements.definition: A thin curved load-carrying surface, or a stabilized lattice idealized as such.
elements.loadPath: Surface forces and bending transfer loading to edges and supports according to geometry and restraints.
limitations: A smooth shape or visually thin skin does not establish structural shell action.
